mappings.note: AIDS expanded plus four prevention methods - reproductive health, C 4.2-LO-5.
A viral and a bacterial STD, plus reasons for using contraceptives - both halves of C 4.2-LO-5.
The role of the male reproductive system and why it is called urinogenital (the urethra is shared) - part-and-function, C 4.2-LO-4.
The process of budding and its sequence in Hydra - budding is named in C 3.2-LO-6.
Parts (a) and (c) are asexual-mode reasoning - regeneration vs reproduction and why spores are thick-walled (C 3.2-LO-6); part (b) is why tubal blocking works as birth control (C 4.2-LO-5).
Labels a germinated seed and gives each part's function. Germination lies past 'seed formation', where C 3.2-LO-7 stops, so no outcome is reached and C 3.2 is the honest level.
Binary vs multiple fission with an example, then the advantages of vegetative reproduction - fission and vegetative propagation, both named in C 3.2-LO-6.

Plants propagated by grafting and the benefits of reproducing through spores - two asexual routes, C 3.2-LO-6. (Stored concept tag 'Pollination and Fertilisation (Plants)' is wrong: neither half involves pollen.)
Four contraceptive methods and their effect on family health and prosperity - both clauses of C 4.2-LO-5.
Regeneration in Planaria and how it differs from reproduction - an asexual mode and its boundary, C 3.2-LO-6.
Two viral and two bacterial STDs and how transmission is prevented - reproductive health, C 4.2-LO-5.

The real demand is Rhizopus: its non-reproductive hyphae, the sporangia and the structure and function of the spores released - an asexual mode, C 3.2-LO-6. Flagged: the stem opens with a stray sentence about condoms that belongs to a different answer, and the stored concept tag 'Reproductive Health and Contraception' matches that stray text, not the question.
Defines pollination, says why it is needed for reproduction in flowering plants, and why cross pollination is preferred - C 3.2-LO-7.
Advantages of sexual over asexual reproduction - the case rests entirely on greater variation, C 3.3-LO-1, not on the mode descriptions of C 3.2-LO-6.
Regeneration of a Planaria cut into three, and another organism that does the same - an asexual mode, C 3.2-LO-6.
Naming the process by which many cut pieces each become an individual (regeneration), with organisms and a schematic - C 3.2-LO-6.
One difference between the modes (C 3.2-LO-6) and then which species survives better and why, which turns on sexual reproduction generating variation (C 3.3-LO-1).

The effect of inaccurate DNA copying and how DNA amount stays constant across generations - chromosome and DNA mechanism, C 3.3. LO-1 is rejected: the sexual-vs-asexual variation contrast is not what is asked.
Part (a) places binary fission and spore formation as asexual modes (C 3.2-LO-6); part (b) asks the advantage of sexual reproduction, which is variation (C 3.3-LO-1).
Names the asexual mode used by six organisms - the enumeration in C 3.2-LO-6.
Six characteristics of sexual reproduction - the sexual side of the C 3.2-LO-6 distinction. Not C 3.3-LO-1, which would need the explicit variation comparison.
What chromosomes are and how their number is held constant in the progeny - chromosome mechanism, C 3.3, not the variation comparison of LO-1.
Significance of reproductive health and the areas that have improved - the second clause of C 4.2-LO-5.
Surgical contraception in men and women - a family-planning method, C 4.2-LO-5.
Defines germination and asks for mislabelled parts of a seedling; germination is past the 'seed formation' end of C 3.2-LO-7, so no outcome is reached. Also figure-dependent.
Fission in Amoeba vs Plasmodium, regeneration vs fragmentation, binary fission vs fragmentation - three contrasts among the asexual modes named in C 3.2-LO-6.
What asexual reproduction is, how it differs from sexual, and another asexual mode used by Hydra - C 3.2-LO-6.
The first half is the importance of DNA copying (C 3.3); the second asks why asexually produced offspring are genetically similar, which needs the asexual-vs-sexual variation contrast of C 3.3-LO-1.
Whether sterilisation protects against STDs, and how AIDS is prevented - family planning weighed against reproductive health, C 4.2-LO-5.
Spore formation in Rhizopus: what it is, what the sporangium holds, why spores are thick-walled - an asexual mode, C 3.2-LO-6.
How the uterus prepares for and nurtures the embryo, and what happens when the egg is not fertilised - the uterus's function, C 4.2-LO-4.
'What do the labelled parts in the diagram work for?' with no figure; the subject cannot be identified, so only the competency C 3.2 is honest. Flagged as figure-dependent.
Identify the type of reproduction and the organism from a diagram. Whatever the figure, the demand is to name an asexual mode and its organism, so C 3.2-LO-6 holds; flagged as figure-dependent.
How chromosome number is kept constant across generations in both asexual and sexual reproducers - chromosome mechanism, C 3.3, not the variation comparison of LO-1.

Functions of the testes, why they sit outside the abdomen, and the hormone behind puberty in boys - all three are the testis's structure and function, C 4.2-LO-4. Preferred over the bare-puberty items at C 4.2 because the answer is an organ's secretion.
What multiple fission is, how it proceeds and an organism that uses it - fission is named in C 3.2-LO-6.

Planaria cut, Spirogyra filament lengthening, sporangia bursting - regeneration, fragmentation and spore formation, all asexual modes in C 3.2-LO-6. (Stored concept tag 'Puberty and Sexual Maturation' is wrong.)
Defines sexual reproduction (C 3.2-LO-6) then asks for four advantages, which are all consequences of greater variation (C 3.3-LO-1).

Reproductive parts of an angiosperm, where they sit, and the structure of the pistil - flower structure inside C 3.2-LO-7. (Stored concept tag 'Human Female Reproductive System' is wrong: this is a flower, not a human.)
Roles of testis, scrotum, vas deferens and prostate, plus two roles of testosterone - part-and-function, C 4.2-LO-4.
Defines reproduction and asks how it stabilises a species' population. No outcome covers the purpose of reproduction, so C 3.2, the competency that names it, is the most specific true code.
Regeneration explained and worked through Hydra - an asexual mode, C 3.2-LO-6.
Part (a) two reasons variation appears in sexual progeny (C 3.3-LO-1); part (b) a labelled flower sequence from pollen to post-fertilisation change (C 3.2-LO-7).
Fission vs fragmentation with an example of each - two asexual modes, both named in C 3.2-LO-6.

Planaria cut into pieces, a Bryophyllum leaf on wet soil, Rhizopus sporangia bursting - regeneration, vegetative propagation and spore formation, all asexual modes in C 3.2-LO-6. (Stored concept tag 'Puberty and Sexual Maturation' is wrong.)
Part (a) the basic requirement for sexual reproduction, i.e. two gametes (C 3.2-LO-6); part (b) its importance in nature, which is the variation it generates (C 3.3-LO-1).
Uterine changes after implantation and after a failed fertilisation - the uterus's function, C 4.2-LO-4.
Chromosome totals and sex chromosomes in human male and female, plus how the number stays constant - chromosome mechanism, C 3.3. Not C 4.2-LO-4: no organ's function is asked.
Four steps of sexual reproduction (C 3.2-LO-6) and its two advantages, which are variation-based (C 3.3-LO-1).
Three reasons reproduction is a defining characteristic of living beings - the purpose of the life process, which no outcome covers; C 3.2 names reproduction and is the honest level.
Vegetative propagation with two advantages and two disadvantages - named verbatim in C 3.2-LO-6. The disadvantage (no variation) is a side note, not the demand, so C 3.3-LO-1 is not cited.
Three pregnancy-prevention techniques, which is female-only, and the family impact - C 4.2-LO-5 on both clauses.
How variations arise and why they aid species survival - the variation half of C 3.3 without the sexual-vs-asexual comparison C 3.3-LO-1 requires.
Regeneration, an organism that shows it, one that does not, and why - an asexual mode and its limits, C 3.2-LO-6.
Contraception defined, two methods, and the effect on family health and prosperity - C 4.2-LO-5.
Placenta and its two major functions - a pregnancy structure and its function, C 4.2-LO-4.
Names the two mammalian gametes and the mode they serve, i.e. sexual reproduction (C 3.2-LO-6), then its advantage, which is variation (C 3.3-LO-1).

Flower diagram labelled ovary/anther/filament/stigma, the anther's function and how plant gametes fuse - the whole C 3.2-LO-7 sequence. (Stored concept tag 'Human Male Reproductive System' is wrong: this is a flower.)
Germination of pollen on the stigma, labelling and how the zygote forms - pollination into fertilisation, C 3.2-LO-7.
Longitudinal section of a flower labelling the pollen-producer, the gamete-carrier, the sticky trap and the part that becomes a fruit - C 3.2-LO-7 end to end.
Part (a) the placenta's role in embryo development (C 4.2-LO-4); part (b) four STDs and the contraceptive that also blocks them (C 4.2-LO-5).
Germination vs fertilisation, pollen vs ovule, and what the ovum, ovary, ovule and perianth become after fertilisation - the fertilisation-to-seed end of C 3.2-LO-7 carries the marks.
Labelled female-system diagram, embryo nutrition and the fate of an unfertilised ovum (C 4.2-LO-4), plus a contraceptive method for the human female (C 4.2-LO-5).

Parts (a) and (c) are the stigma, the pollen tube and seed formation in a flower (C 3.2-LO-7); part (b) asks two changes at puberty in a girl, which reaches no outcome and sits at the competency C 4.2. (Stored concept tag 'Spore Formation' is wrong.)

Three demands: the male parts producing sperm, fluid, low temperature and the shared passage (C 4.2-LO-4); an STD and how to avoid it (C 4.2-LO-5); and two puberty changes in boys, which reaches no outcome and sits at C 4.2. (Stored concept tag 'Spore Formation' is wrong.)
Yeast needing sugar, the benefit of spores, and regeneration vs fragmentation - three asexual-mode points, all C 3.2-LO-6.

Part (a) three advantages of sexual over asexual reproduction, which are variation-based (C 3.3-LO-1); part (b) the fate of the fertilised egg in the human female, i.e. implantation in the uterus (C 4.2-LO-4).

Part (a) a plant propagated by leaves (C 3.2-LO-6); parts (b)-(e) are STD causative organisms, tubal ligation, the IUCD and the falling sex ratio, all reproductive health and family planning (C 4.2-LO-5).
Part (a) two reasons variation appears in sexual progeny (C 3.3-LO-1); part (b) a labelled flower with pollen reaching the ovule and post-fertilisation change (C 3.2-LO-7).
Flower diagram with ovary/anther/filament/stigma, how plant gametes fuse and male vs female gamete differences - C 3.2-LO-7. (Stored concept tag 'Human Male Reproductive System' is wrong.)
Parts (a)-(c) label the female tract and trace the uterine lining (C 4.2-LO-4); part (d) asks the surgical birth-control methods (C 4.2-LO-5).

Parts (a) and (b) are fertilisation and double fertilisation in a flowering plant and what becomes fruit and seed (C 3.2-LO-7); part (c) contrasts unicellular with multicellular modes of reproduction (C 3.2-LO-6).

Three distinct demands: budding in Hydra (C 3.2-LO-6); whether fertilisation can occur without pollination and post-fertilisation change in a flower (C 3.2-LO-7); and what the copper-T is and where it sits (C 4.2-LO-5).
Reproduction in Plasmodium and Leishmania, i.e. multiple and binary fission (C 3.2-LO-6); sorting flowers into bisexual and unisexual (C 3.2-LO-7); and the function of the male urethra (C 4.2-LO-4).
Male-system diagram, the timing of ovulation and what menopause is - all part-and-function of the human reproductive system, C 4.2-LO-4.
What asexual reproduction is, four of its methods, and binary fission in Amoeba - C 3.2-LO-6.
Male-system diagram plus the function and location of the testes - part-and-function, C 4.2-LO-4.

How oral pills and condoms prevent pregnancy, and the misuse of surgical birth control together with the government's response - family planning and reproductive health at the social level, C 4.2-LO-5.
A bisexual flower and its pistil, a labelled section showing pollen germination, and pollination vs fertilisation - the whole C 3.2-LO-7 sequence.
Germination of pollen on the stigma and the post-fertilisation changes in a flower - C 3.2-LO-7.

Part (b) asks how potato and Bryophyllum reproduce vegetatively, which is named in C 3.2-LO-6. Part (a), labelling a germinating seed, is past 'seed formation' and reaches no outcome, so no second code is added.
Listing STDs and naming a safe-sex method for both partners - reproductive health, C 4.2-LO-5.
Male-system diagram, why the testes sit outside, the testicular hormone and the two accessory glands - part-and-function, C 4.2-LO-4.
Female-system diagram with oviduct, ovary, uterus, cervix and the function of uterus and oviduct - C 4.2-LO-4.

Menstruation and how the embryo is nourished carry most of the marks (C 4.2-LO-4); wind as a pollinating agent is C 3.2-LO-7; condoms preventing pregnancy is C 4.2-LO-5. The fourth sub-part on the benefit of variation is the smallest and is left uncoded to stay within three codes.
Reproduction in Hydra (budding) and Planaria (regeneration), with the processes named - C 3.2-LO-6.
Causes of human population explosion and how it can be checked - family planning at the social level, C 4.2-LO-5.
Pollination, how it occurs and how it leads to fertilisation - the C 3.2-LO-7 sequence.
Part (a) three features distinguishing sexual from asexual reproduction (C 3.2-LO-6); part (b) why variation appears in sexually produced offspring (C 3.3-LO-1).

Part (b), the roles of gametes and zygote in sexually reproducing organisms, is the scorable demand and sits with the sexual side of C 3.2-LO-6. Part (a) needs a figure that is not supplied; flagged as figure-dependent.
Sectional view of the human female system, where the egg develops and where fertilisation happens - part-and-function, C 4.2-LO-4.
Part (a) the placenta's function (C 4.2-LO-4); part (b) four ways of preventing pregnancy with two advantages (C 4.2-LO-5).
Names the female parts that produce eggs, host fertilisation and receive the zygote, then follows the implanted zygote - part-and-function, C 4.2-LO-4.

Parts (a) and the first half of (b) are unisexual/bisexual flowers and post-fertilisation change (C 3.2-LO-7); the last clause on how DNA amount stays constant across generations is chromosome mechanism (C 3.3).

Testis as sperm-producer and hormone source, uterine changes with and without a zygote, the site of fertilisation and implantation, and embryo nourishment - every part is human part-and-function, C 4.2-LO-4.
Defines fragmentation and regeneration and asks whether they are the same - fragmentation is named in C 3.2-LO-6 and regeneration is its near neighbour.

Five definitions split across two outcomes: vegetative propagation, regeneration and binary fission are asexual modes (C 3.2-LO-6); fertilisation and menstruation are human reproductive functions (C 4.2-LO-4).
Labelled flower parts, what pollination is and why it matters, how fertilisation occurs and what becomes seed and fruit - the whole C 3.2-LO-7 sequence.
Identifying a Bryophyllum-type leaf, the method it uses (vegetative propagation), its advantages and other plants grown that way - C 3.2-LO-6.

Parts (a) and (b) are about variation over time and offspring being similar but not identical, i.e. DNA-copying and heredity (C 3.3); part (c) is binary fission differing between Amoeba and Leishmania (C 3.2-LO-6).
Five sub-parts split three ways: testosterone release (C 4.2-LO-4); pollen on the stigma and egg-sperm fusion in the plant sequence (C 3.2-LO-7); Planaria cut and Bryophyllum notch buds (C 3.2-LO-6).

Fission in Amoeba vs Plasmodium, fragmentation vs regeneration, Hydra vs Bryophyllum buds and vegetative propagation vs spore formation are all asexual modes (C 3.2-LO-6); pollen tube vs style is flower anatomy (C 3.2-LO-7).
Functions of ovary, oviduct and uterus, plus the structure and function of the placenta - the exact demand of C 4.2-LO-4.
Vegetative propagation, three advantages and which listed plants use it - named verbatim in C 3.2-LO-6.
